AK.quote: Any nonvenomous reptile   Class Reptilia   (crocodile, alligator, snake, turtle, or lizard)
AK.note: Alaska's clean list turns entirely on venom.

AL.note: Not native to Alabama, so it's an ordinary nonvenomous pet reptile rather than wildlife needing a possession-limit accounting; no restriction was found.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: New World Colubrid Snakes (in part) (Genera: Bogertophis, Drymarchon, Drymobius, Lampropeltis, Pantherophis, Phrynonax, Pituophis, Pseudelaphe, Senticolis, Spilotes) except species native to Arkansas
AR.note: Named on the unrestricted list by genus; the native-species exception in that entry doesn't reach the California kingsnake since it isn't an Arkansas species.

AZ.note: The California kingsnake's range reaches into parts of Arizona, so the same hunting/fishing-license framework that governs wild take of native reptiles applies there, but simple possession of a lawfully-acquired one isn't restricted, and it isn't on Arizona's no-open-season list.

CA.note: Not on the Fish & Game Code § 671 restricted species list, so owning one is unrestricted. Wild collection of a California kingsnake specifically requires a sportfishing license and is capped at a 4-per-day bag/possession limit; unlike the common garter snake, there are no county-level closures for this species.

CO.note: Colorado clears the genus Lampropeltis by name except for the western milksnake and the speckled kingsnake, neither of which is the California kingsnake.

CT.note: Outside all four of Connecticut's wild-animal categories, which reach only specific dangerous mammals, dangerous reptiles, native birds/amphibians, and state-listed species.

DC.quote: Non-venomous snakes, fish, and turtles, traditionally kept in the home for pleasure rather than for commercial purposes
DC.note: A California kingsnake fits this exemption from DC's general wild-animal ban squarely.

DE.note: A live reptile not native to or generally found in Delaware needs a permit from the Department of Agriculture before it may be brought into the state, possessed, sold, or exhibited. The California kingsnake, a Pacific coast species, is exotic to Delaware.

FL.note: Not a reptile of concern; that category is built around large invasive constrictors, monitors, and tegus. Ordinary nonvenomous colubrids like the California kingsnake need no license as a personal pet.

GA.note: Georgia's wild-animal license rule doesn't name any snake at all, and the California kingsnake isn't Georgia native wildlife, so it falls outside both the wild-animal license scheme and the native-species possession restriction that reaches Georgia's own native kingsnake population.

HI.note: Hawaii's snake ban reaches every species in the suborder, kingsnakes included, with no pet-keeping permit available.

IA.note: The squamate half of Iowa's 'dangerous wild animal' definition is exhaustively enumerated (monitors, helodermatids, venomous families, a short list of giant constrictors); a kingsnake is none of them.

ID.quote: non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians
ID.note: Idaho's test is venom, not species.

IL.note: Illinois's Dangerous Animals Act is a closed list of big cats and never reaches ordinary colubrids. Illinois is a home-rule state, so a municipality can still restrict snake ownership on its own.

IN.note: Indiana's Wild Animal Possession Permit reaches venomous reptiles and large crocodilians, not ordinary nonvenomous snakes like a kingsnake.

KS.note: The only reptiles Kansas regulates are non-native venomous snakes.

KY.note: Kentucky's inherently-dangerous-wildlife list reaches Colubridae only when the snake is venomous.

LA.note: Louisiana's prohibited nonnative reptile list is built around crocodilians, tegus, monitors, the green iguana, and a short list of large or venomous snakes; ordinary colubrids like the kingsnake aren't on it.

MA.note: The whole genus is named on the license-exemption list, California kingsnake included.

MD.note: Not a Maryland native, so the state's native-reptile possession permit doesn't apply, and it's absent from the § 10-621 dangerous-animal list.

ME.cite: Unrestricted Species list, Serpentes (Captive Bred Origin Only)
ME.quote: All Species in Genus Lampropeltis (Kingsnakes And Milk Snakes) Except for: Lampropeltis herrerae; Lampropeltis triangulum triangulum
ME.note: The whole genus is cleared except two named species, neither of which is the California kingsnake.

MN.note: Minnesota's regulated-animal statute reaches cats, bears, and non-human primates. No reptile appears in it.

MO.note: Class I, Missouri's permit tier for nonvenomous reptiles, reaches only species native to Missouri. The California kingsnake isn't one, so it falls outside that requirement.

MS.note: Mississippi's inherently-dangerous list is entirely mammalian; no reptile is restricted at any size.

MT.quote: all nonnative tropical and subtropical species of nonvenomous snakes not on the controlled or prohibited lists in the families: ...(v) Colubridae (modern snakes);

NC.note: North Carolina's only statewide exotic-animal statute covers venomous reptiles. Everything else is left to county ordinance.

ND.note: No reptile appears anywhere in North Dakota's captive wildlife chapter.

NE.note: Not endangered or threatened, and not one of the specifically prohibited carnivore families; an ordinary exotic pet reptile in Nebraska.

NH.quote: Reptiles, exotic, except: a. Alligator (Alligatoridae, spp); b. Crocodile (Crocodylidae, spp); and c. Venomous reptiles, other than the Western Hognose Snake;
NH.note: An exotic, nonvenomous reptile like the California kingsnake clears New Hampshire's noncontrolled list.

NJ.note: Absent from the potentially dangerous species table, which limits its snakes to venomous families plus boomslang, twig snakes, African kraits, and anaconda.

NM.note: New Mexico sorts exotic wildlife into Groups I through IV by danger level; the California kingsnake wasn't named in the regulation text located, and an unlisted species defaults to Group IV, whose actual requirements weren't confirmed in this research.

NV.note: Nevada's unprotected-reptile category covers most kingsnakes, though the state singles out California kingsnakes lacking a continuous banded/ringed pattern from head to vent as the specific unprotected form, so pattern can matter for certain individuals.

NY.note: New York's native-snake statute names its own indigenous species by common name, including the eastern milk snake (Lampropeltis triangulum); the California kingsnake is a Pacific coast species and isn't one of them, so it doesn't inherit the native-species possession permit that a New York garter snake needs. No other statute restricts it.

OH.note: Ohio's restricted-snake list is three venomous families plus two named rear-fanged species plus large constrictors twelve feet and up. A kingsnake is none of them.

OK.note: Non-indigenous reptiles are exempt from Oklahoma's import, breeder's-license, and permit requirements outright, and the California kingsnake isn't indigenous to Oklahoma.

OR.quote: Individuals of Lampropeltis getula, L. zonata and Pituophis catenifer that are morphologically distinct from native species.
OR.note: Oregon's kingsnake clearance, written under the older taxonomy in which the California kingsnake was classified as Lampropeltis getula californiae, only reaches individuals 'morphologically distinct from native species' -- in practice, a recognizable color or pattern morph rather than a wild-type-looking snake. Wild-caught, native-looking kingsnakes and their offspring aren't covered.

PA.note: Fish and Boat Commission possession rules apply only to species native to Pennsylvania. The California kingsnake isn't one, so it isn't reached by that chapter at all.

RI.note: Named directly on Rhode Island's exempt Colubridae list.

SC.note: South Carolina exempts reptiles as a class from the import permit.

SD.note: South Dakota's possession-permit list covers mammals only; reptiles fall under separate Game, Fish & Parks rules.

TN.note: Not native to Tennessee, so a California kingsnake is Class III: a nonpoisonous, non-native reptile that needs no registration.

TX.note: Texas's dangerous wild animal statute doesn't reach ordinary snakes. Legal statewide, though some cities restrict snakes by ordinance.

UT.note: Falls under Utah's non-controlled reptile framework, the same one that clears the garter snake: up to three may be possessed without a certificate of registration, more with one from the Wildlife Board.

VA.note: Virginia's special-permit table works species by species and contains no reptile relevant to a kingsnake.

VT.note: Vermont requires an Importation & Possession Permit for any wild animal not on its Unrestricted Wild Animals List. This research could not confirm whether the California kingsnake appears on that list.

WA.note: The only colubrid Washington restricts is the boomslang.

WI.note: As a non-native species, the California kingsnake sits outside Wisconsin's native-reptile possession cap and can be kept the way corn snakes and ball pythons are, without a DNR license. Bringing one in from out of state calls for a DATCP animal import permit and health paperwork.

WV.note: The only reptiles West Virginia's dangerous-wild-animal guidance points at are large constrictors, venomous snakes, and crocodilians.

WY.note: Not venomous, and not on Wyoming's Section 8 prohibited list.
